brief.head: Not wood, not stones
brief.text: Ajay Shah adapts Mark Antony’s line from *Julius Caesar* into an economist’s slogan: people are not fools, and they will optimise around whatever the state does. {092-C04}

brief.head: Why, what and how
brief.text: Amit Varma borrowed the subsidiarity principle: decide the why at the top, the what a level below and the how locally, where the best information lies. {092-C13}

brief.head: Part of the product
brief.text: Communication is not advertising but part of governance, Amit Varma argued: words matched by deeds build the trust that drives the economy. {092-C09}

brief.head: Legitimacy, next time

brief.head: Pouring the concrete
brief.text: No law truly binds the state, Ajay Shah said; any act can be amended. Policies last only when a community of guardians watches over them. {092-C14}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on why rules beat strongmen
lead.head: Strong rules, not strong rulers
body: All of us start out, Ajay Shah said, as “little clueless children” who want a strong man to run the state, and expect a Ram Rajya. “All of growing up is about understanding how this actually doesn’t work well,” he said.
In this episode, Shah and Amit Varma took up what Shah called a great contribution by “my clan of economists” to political philosophy: rules, not discretion.
The economists’ claim cuts against intuition. “The state becomes more effective, not less, when it shackles its own hands with rules and takes away discretion,” Shah said. {092-C01}
## Three arguments

Shah built the case in three stages. The first is public choice theory: the strongman is not a Ram but “a regular guy”, with wants and needs, who makes mistakes like everybody else. Living under his absolute power is “nothing less than a nightmare”.

The second comes from public administration. A strongman’s minions become little tyrants, so even an autocrat wants rules to bind them. Julius Caesar, Shah said, wrote laws for everyone beneath him while staying above them himself.
The third is the economists’ own: the state gains power by giving up discretion. That offends the machismo of most civil servants, Shah said, who like bestowing favours on supplicants.
Varma added James Buchanan’s test: design a system so strong that if the worst person imaginable is in charge, “they can’t do much damage”.
## Credibility as power
The episode turned on a 1977 paper by the Norwegian economist Finn Kydland and the American economist Edward Prescott, *Rules Rather than Discretion*. Both, Shah said, won the Nobel Prize for it.

Its lesson is that people watch the state and adjust. Raise a promised low tax rate on global firms whose factories are already built, Shah said, and the move may be popular, but every firm will price in the risk for years. “The state loses power by being opportunistic.” {092-S03}
A central bank faces the same test. It must deliver its inflation target, Shah argued, whether there is an election, a crisis or a drought.
“In the world of inflation targeting, there’s a beautiful slogan,” he said. “We say that say what you will do and then do what you just said.” {092-C07}
Hence what Shah called handcuffs as commitment devices: a state short of credibility deliberately makes breaking its own rules unpleasant for itself. {092-C08}
## The road to growth

For the hosts, the stakes are India’s poverty. Growth, Shah said, comes from high-productivity firms that take years to build, and into which people commit “their money, their intensity, their passion, their time, their children”.
Each expropriation and each sudden change of rules teaches them to hold back. “All these fears add up to a wet blanket,” he said. The result is low GDP growth. {092-C12}
The same logic, Shah argued, runs through contracts between firms, criminal sentencing, treaties and parenting.
Varma turned the idea on himself. As a teenager he was “a rebel without restraints”. Today, with rules for sleep, meals and exercise, he is “a rebel with rules”.
Shah summed it up: “Be quiet and predictable in your life, so that you can be explosive and creative in your ideas.”
Varma had one question. “Have you ever considered Twitter?”

second.label: Ancient Rome
second.head: Laws for all but Caesar
second.deck: Ajay Shah on the strongman who wrote rules for everyone beneath him
body: Julius Caesar was no democrat, Ajay Shah said. He destroyed the Roman Republic just as Rome had started learning how to disperse power. Yet Shah counts him among the greatest human beings and thinkers who ever lived. {092-S05}

Running the Roman Empire, Caesar did not want his minions choosing how to wield his coercive power, each becoming a local tyrant. So he started writing laws and process manuals, so that all of them would act in ways he defined.

Shah called this rule by law: Caesar had arbitrary power, but wanted everyone else to work in a predictable, rules-based way. {092-C03} Amit Varma set it apart from rule of law, in which even the ruler is bound.

quote.text: Julius Caesar destroyed the republic. I also happen to consider him one of the greatest human beings who ever lived.

second.caption: Julius Caesar’s laws

third.head: Drunk on a 1977 paper
body: “Ajay Shah reads papers the way other adolescent boys watch porn,” Amit Varma told listeners. One paper at nine at night becomes forty by four in the morning. {092-J04}
This time the paper was Finn Kydland and Edward Prescott’s, from 1977, which Shah first met in his first-year PhD coursework, when he was “a happy, giddy child”.
Preparing for this episode, Shah had an anxiety attack: had he forgotten something? So he went back and reread the paper that morning, and was partly happy to find he knew it all.

But the rereading did more. “I also just got a little drunk with happiness,” he said, “because just the whole memory, the feeling of being in first year PhD and discovering these things for the first time came back to me.” {092-S02}
third.caption: rereading Kydland and Prescott

p2.title: Rules, not discretion
p2.deck: The case against the strongman, from Caesar’s minions to the parent who cannot bring himself to punish

sections.label: The strongman
sections.head: Wanted: a weak leader
sections.caption: the trouble with strongmen
body: Our pull towards strong leaders is old, Amit Varma said. Our instincts were shaped in prehistoric tribes of at most a hundred and fifty people, where top-down thinking worked. {#tribes} The attraction to a strongman “is baked into us and we have to fight it”.

Ajay Shah built his case in stages. Public choice theory says the strongman is an ordinary person with flaws, so his absolute power is a nightmare; the remedy is checks and balances, rule of law and dispersed power. Public administration adds that even a strongman needs rules, because all his minions become tyrants in their own way.
## What weak means
Shah wants weak leaders, and Varma clarified the word. It does not mean weak of character or intellect. It means leaders “whose ability to act on their wishes is restrained by a set of laws”.

Varma cited James Buchanan, one of the guiding lights of public choice theory: build a system so solid that the worst person imaginable, “whether it is Hitler or anyone”, can do little harm at the top. {092-C02}
Shah offered a test of his own. When someone asks the strongman for a wish, can he grant it? A good country, he said, is one where the strongman can do very little. {092-J11}
~ The economists’ argument, Shah warned, offends most civil servants, whose machismo says: “I get to decide.”

quote.text: if the worst person you can imagine is in charge, they can’t do much damage.

sections.label: Monetary policy
sections.head: Four per cent, no matter what
sections.caption: anchoring inflation at 4 per cent
body: In a good world, Ajay Shah said, a central bank promises stable inflation and delivers it, cutting rates when the economy is in deep trouble and raising them when it overheats.

Firms whose minds are anchored on 4 per cent inflation stop raising prices at every dearer raw material or local wage rise. Bond markets settle too. “If you have confidence about inflation for the next 25 years, then you have confidence on what interest rate you require for a 25-year loan or a 25-year bond,” Shah said. {#bonds}
## A bleeding heart’s mistake

In the 1970s oil shock, Shah said, American policymakers saw people paying more for petrol and unemployment rising, and chose not to add to the misery by raising rates. A little inflation for some time, they thought. {092-S06}
Firms and bond markets learnt that inflation was not guaranteed. Behaviour across the economy changed, in ways harmful for growth.
India’s law now holds the RBI accountable for 4 per cent. {#rbiact} But the regime is new and the RBI’s record “middling”, Shah said, so anchoring minds will take decades. {092-C05}
~ Amit Varma noted that Shah had pushed for inflation targeting from the 1990s, and that it took more than a decade and a half to become law.

quote.text: But the thing is, once you do this, you have unhinged the expectations of the economy.

sections.label: Focus on rules
sections.head: Manual labour
sections.caption: handcuffs as commitment devices
body: The primitive model of governance, Ajay Shah said, is a person who looks at each situation and decides. Finn Kydland and Edward Prescott move the real work into designing the rule: if state X arises, do Y. {092-C06}
Officials then simply live up to “a publicly stated manual”. The debates worth having are about rules, such as whether to target the exchange rate or inflation.

Rules may be complex. A bond could, by its own terms, pay no interest in a year when real GDP growth is negative. What is not on is skipping a payment after the fact. “You’re allowed to go complexity, but you’re not allowed to expropriate people,” Shah said. {092-C10}
## The price of a broken promise

A state short of credibility should wear handcuffs. Shah’s design for a monetary policy committee gives the governor, the channel for political pressure, one vote among five, beside four independent economists. {092-R03}

In New Zealand, he said, central bankers get a bonus for hitting the target and lose money when they miss, all by press release. {#newzealand} A missed target can also mean a mea culpa letter setting out what went wrong.
~ Such devices work, Shah said, because the leaders of such organisations care most about the respect of their peers.

quote.text: So the work of doing public policy is actually more meta. It is about imagining one rule at a time.

sections.label: Growth
sections.head: Where great firms come from
sections.caption: rules as the machinery of growth
body: India is still poor, Amit Varma said, with hundreds of millions of people in poverty, and growth is the way out. What do rules have to do with it?

They are of first-order importance, Ajay Shah answered. Growth comes from high-productivity firms controlling large amounts of labour and capital, and such firms come out of the “toil, sweat, and tears” of people who spend years building them.
This is not a quick startup chasing an exit at 10X, he said, but the hard work of building large, complex organisations.
## The private sector is watching

Whether anyone makes that effort depends on the state. The private sector, Shah said, is not stupid: it watches patterns. Expropriate one person today, and others fear they will be next. Create a monopoly PSU in one business, and others fear one in theirs.

Foreign firms worry that a national champion will get the government to rig the game. The fears add up, Shah said: people hold globally diversified assets, wait and see, and GDP growth stays low. {092-C12}
~ India needs this more than rich countries, Shah argued, given its institutional mistrust: officials should face daily press conferences and unscripted town halls. {092-C11}

quote.text: Firms don’t come out of thin air.

sections.label: Amit’s thoughts
sections.head: Orders, and when to break them
sections.caption: rules that leave room to adapt
body: Amit Varma raised doubts. Rules can be rigid: India, he said, citing an earlier discussion of Shah’s, has one Maggi and one Kit Kat, while Japan has thirty varieties of Kit Kat. {092-J14}

He recalled General Sagat Singh, who at Nathu La and Cho La disobeyed an order from high command because he understood local conditions, which later helped India enormously. Varma’s tentative fix: build complexity into the rules, so they say when discretion applies. {092-S08}
Ajay Shah agreed. Great militaries split strategy, operations and tactics, each level owning its own sphere. In government, the answer is decentralisation.
## Kodak’s straitjacket

Rules can also stifle firms, Varma said. Citing Clayton Christensen’s *The Innovator’s Dilemma*, he noted that Kodak had the know-how for digital photography but could not make the move. Google, in the early 2000s, let staff spend time on passion projects. {092-S09}

Shah agreed about firms. But a city like Liverpool, he said, has wanted the same basics for hundreds of years: streets, parks, solid waste management, water and sanitation. The exception is military affairs, where Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has set off an innovation spiral.
~ Could lost trust be rebuilt? Policy lasts, Shah said, only when an intellectual community guards it, not when economists “whisper in the ears of Aurangzeb”. {092-J05}

quote.text: You have to follow orders, otherwise a whole edifice can collapse. But at the same time you also need that local discretion.

sections.label: Beyond economics
sections.head: Bullies, judges and parents
sections.caption: contracts, courts, treaties and children
body: The framework reaches far beyond economics, Ajay Shah said, starting with contracts between firms.

Many large Indian firms buying a humble part believe a hundred suppliers are desperate to sell to them. {#vendors} So they drive hard bargains, extract working-capital credit from small firms and practise gundagiri, breaking contracts when it suits them.

Small firms build that into their expectations and shade their bids upward, so the bully pays more than firms that behave well. Opportunism may win one procurement, Shah said. “But like what about the future?” {092-S10}
## Courts, treaties and homes

In criminal law he favours sentencing guidelines, because wide discretion opens a Pandora’s box of doubts about fair play and tempts criminals to bet on leniency. A strongman who walks out of a treaty is cheered at home, but every partner learns his country cannot be trusted. {092-C15}

Then parenting. No parent wants to punish a child, Shah said, so when the moment comes it is tempting to let it go. That is how a parent loses credibility, and children raised on moods learn to game the parent. {092-S11}
~ What works, he said, is predictable rules that evolve gradually, not micromanagement, and not a yes today and a no tomorrow.

quote.text: And yet, when you do that, actually you’ve lost all your credibility, you’ve lost your commitment.

side.boxText: Finn Kydland and Edward Prescott’s *Rules Rather than Discretion: The Inconsistency of Optimal Plans* came out of the rational expectations revolution. It taught economists to take credibility and commitment seriously, and, Ajay Shah said, it won both authors the Nobel Prize. {092-R01}

contQuote.text: It is wise and efficient for the state to shed discretion, to shed power, to lose power, to create a series of provisions and mechanisms through which violating the rule will become unpleasant for the state.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: A tax grab, a poker table, a finance minister and a reformed rebel

stories.start: let's consider the taxation of corporations. Okay. So a great uh success story
stories.end: the policy, the policymaker, the state, becomes less effective by being more opportunistic
stories.caption: the Irish tax grab
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s thought experiment on a tax raid that backfires
stories.head: The hostages have long memories
body: Ireland, Ajay Shah said, set a very low corporate tax rate. Global companies chose to put factories and offices there, and it powered great Irish growth. He would recommend the same for India: very low corporate tax, ideally zero.
Then he imagined a bad turn: an economic downturn, or a great earthquake, with the people suffering. A policymaker says the 5 per cent rate must rise, just for two or three years.
Shah called him “the clever policy maker, it’s Indian IAS level of IQ”. {092-J03} The factories are already built, so the firms are hostages. They can’t leave. Why not grab a little of their money?
The move is popular. The press praises it. It might even win an election. Until the 1970s, Shah said, this kind of reasoning was normal among economists.

But firms invest on five-, 10- and 25-year horizons. A firm that built its factory expecting an 8 per cent return on equity in dollars now finds it is 6 per cent, and its calculations are upended. {#roe}

Worse, it now assumes it can be socked again. Every future spreadsheet carries a higher tax rate as a safety factor, or a higher required return to pay for the risk, and for years the low tax rate loses its pull. {092-S03}
~ People have long memories, Shah said. They remember the period when the state “stole so much money from the companies”, and wonder whether it will do it again.
stories.why: Opportunism looks like a free win, but it spends the credibility that made the policy work in the first place. People are not fools, Shah said: they look ahead, watch the policymaker and adjust. {092-C04}

stories.start: So you know what this reminds me of? This reminds me of poker.
stories.end: And the world changes with every action every individual takes
stories.caption: the four-bet
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a lesson from the poker table
stories.head: The four-bet that meant nothing
body: Most poker, Amit Varma said, is exploitative. You spot a mistake the table keeps making, such as folding too much, and adjust to profit from it.
The trap is assuming the table will not adjust back. That, he said, is “why exploitative poker is also automatically exploitable poker”. {092-S04}

In the 2000s, Varma read a canonical poker book which said a four-bet, a re-raise of a re-raise, is almost always aces. By the time he was a professional, it was often nothing at all. “Everybody read the book,” Ajay Shah said, “and said, Oh, I can exploit this.”
~ Varma took the lesson to taxes. In the 1970s, he said, Indira Gandhi had a top tax rate of, he thought, 97 per cent, and India was not a booming economy. {#ninetyseven}
stories.why: People respond to your actions, Varma said, so the world does not stand still while you exploit it. Raise a tax rate too far and collections can actually fall, because people change their behaviour.

stories.start: It strikes me that building trust can take decades, but losing trust
stories.end: but all behaving with the best interests of the nation at heart
stories.caption: retrospective taxation
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on how India’s growth episode went bust
stories.head: Taxed today for yesterday
body: It takes decades to build trust and an instant to lose it, Amit Varma said, and India’s growth episode from 1991 to 2011 showed how. {092-S07}

After the terror attacks in Bombay, Manmohan Singh moved his most capable man, P. Chidambaram, from finance to the home ministry. Sonia Gandhi gave finance to Pranab Mukherjee, and Singh, who had health issues, did not take it himself.

Varma called Mukherjee a “wild evil courtier” with no knowledge of economics, who came up with one disastrous measure after another. The worst was retrospective taxation: telling companies that new tax rules applied to the past too, so they owed dues. {#retro}
~ It destroys trust, he said, especially among foreign investors, whom India needs. In those twenty years, different parties had governed with the nation’s interests at heart. {#parties}
stories.why: Retrospective tax is the ultimate discretionary ambush, and Varma feared India would take years, if not decades, to recover from it. Bad policy is bad policy, he said, whichever political party is in power.

stories.start: When I was young I was a rebel without restraints, right?
stories.end: which automatically then enables me to be at my best
stories.caption: the rebel with rules
stories.kicker: Amit Varma turns the episode’s idea on himself
stories.head: The rebel goes to bed early
body: At fifteen, sixteen and seventeen, Amit Varma said, he was a rebel without a cause, “or if we wish to alliterate, a rebel without restraints”. {092-J01}
He stayed up late, worked three days in a row, drank beer with friends when he felt like it, skipped exercise and ate anything. All of it, he now thinks, worked against rebellion. {092-S01}

Today he tries to sleep at least eight hours, eat at predictable times and watch his diet, especially after a recent health episode. {#sleep} On exercise, he admits, it is “do as I say, don’t do as I do”.

~ The rules are a scaffolding to take off from, he said, like the algorithms that let Elon Musk’s rocket be caught on its return. Just as a constitution constrains the state, not the people, his rules constrain his bad habits.

quote.text: Those rules aren’t constraints. They help us become the best version of ourselves.

stories.postscript: Ajay Shah’s biceps, Varma pointed out on camera, came from a rules-based regime, not from whatever exercise he felt like. {092-J07}

quiz.q: In Ajay Shah’s three-stage case against the strongman, what is the economists’ own argument?
quiz.a: That the state becomes more effective, not less, when it shackles its own hands.

quiz.q: What separates rule by law, as practised by Julius Caesar, from rule of law?
quiz.a: Rule by law binds everyone except the ruler; rule of law binds the ruler too.

quiz.q: Which line from Shakespeare’s *Julius Caesar* did Ajay Shah turn into his economics slogan?
quiz.a: “You are not wood, you are not stones, but men”, adding “you will optimize”.

quiz.q: In Shah’s design for a monetary policy committee, how many of five votes face political pressure?
quiz.a: Just one, the governor’s; the other four belong to independent private economists.

quiz.q: According to a canonical poker book Amit Varma read in the 2000s, what did a four-bet mean?
quiz.a: Almost always aces, though by his professional days it often meant nothing at all.

quiz.q: Which single exercise does Ajay Shah recommend for anyone too lazy to do more?
quiz.a: Rowing on a machine, cardio that uses about 80 to 85 per cent of muscles.
